noteRef.topicTitle: Structure and functions in living organisms

specPoints.text: know the similarities and differences in the structure of plant and animal cells

primer.text: Animal and plant cells share the core eukaryotic kit, but each adds its own extras. This note lists the subcellular structures of an animal cell, the three additions plants make, and the comparison table that turns those lists into exam answers — the similarities AND the differences, side by side.

lessons.title: The animal-cell inventory
lessons.opening: An animal cell runs on five named structures: a nucleus holding the genetic material, a cell membrane deciding what enters and leaves, mitochondria for aerobic respiration, ribosomes building proteins, and the jelly-like cytoplasm where reactions happen. Some of these are too small for a light microscope and only appear under an electron microscope.
keyPoints: The nucleus contains the cell's genetic material.
The cell membrane controls what enters and leaves the cell.
Mitochondria are the site of aerobic respiration.
Ribosomes are the site of protein synthesis.
Cytoplasm is the jelly-like substance where chemical reactions take place.

low.restatement: Animal cell: nucleus, membrane, mitochondria, ribosomes, cytoplasm — five structures to name and one job each.
low.analogy: Think of a small workshop: the nucleus is the manager's office, the membrane the door policy, mitochondria the generator, ribosomes the assembly bench, cytoplasm the floor everything stands on.
low.examPointer: Pair each structure with its function in one line — 'mitochondria: site of aerobic respiration' is a complete mark.

medium.restatement: Each structure's function follows from its design: the membrane's selective barrier role, the mitochondrion's folded surface for respiration, ribosomes as the protein-assembly site.
medium.analogy: A factory floor plan explains the workflow — where a machine sits tells you what it does.
medium.examPointer: Electron-microscope resolution is a favourite twist: ribosomes and detailed mitochondria need it, so say which microscope an image came from.

check.stem: Which structure holds the genetic material of an animal cell?

options.explanation: The nucleus contains the genetic material.
Cytoplasm hosts reactions, not the genome.
The membrane controls entry and exit.

check.stem: Which structure is the site of aerobic respiration?

options.explanation: Animal cells lack the permanent vacuole.

check.stem: What does the cell membrane do?

options.text: Controls what enters and leaves the cell

options.explanation: Cell sap sits in the plant vacuole.

check.stem: Which instrument reveals cellular structures that a light microscope cannot show?

options.explanation: The note flags structures only visible with electron microscopy.

check.stem: Where in an animal cell do most chemical reactions happen?

options.explanation: The membrane controls traffic, not the reaction bulk.

check.stem: Name the structure that is the site of protein synthesis.
check.modelAnswer: Ribosomes — the site of protein synthesis.

check.stem: State the function of the cytoplasm.
check.modelAnswer: It is the jelly-like substance where chemical reactions take place.

check.stem: Explain why mitochondria and ribosomes are described with DIFFERENT jobs even though both are tiny subcellular structures.
check.modelAnswer: Each structure is built for its task: mitochondria provide the internal surface and enzymes for aerobic respiration, while ribosomes assemble amino acids into proteins, so one is the power plant and the other the assembly bench rather than interchangeable parts.

check.stem: A cell sample shows dense mitochondria but very few ribosomes. Which activity would this cell favour, and what does the scarcity of ribosomes suggest?
check.modelAnswer: Dense mitochondria point to high energy demand through aerobic respiration; few ribosomes suggest little protein manufacture, so the cell imports rather than builds most of its proteins.

lessons.title: Plant additions and the comparison table
lessons.opening: Plant cells carry everything an animal cell has, plus three structures: a cellulose cell wall that gives shape and protection, a permanent vacuole of cell sap that keeps the cell turgid, and — in leaf and stem tissue — chloroplasts for photosynthesis. The comparison table collects both lists so the shared and unique features sit side by side.
keyPoints: Plant cells add a cellulose cell wall that gives shape and protection.
The permanent vacuole holds cell sap and keeps the cell turgid.
Chloroplasts appear in leaf and stem cells and are the site of photosynthesis.
Nucleus, cytoplasm, membrane, mitochondria and ribosomes sit in BOTH cell types.

low.restatement: Plant = animal kit + cellulose wall + permanent vacuole + (in leaves and stems) chloroplasts.
low.analogy: A plant cell is an animal cell that built a fence (wall), installed a water tank (vacuole) and added solar panels (chloroplasts).
low.examPointer: Learn the table's three plant-only rows — they are the differences examiners ask for.

medium.restatement: The three additions map to three plant problems: support without skeletons (wall), water balance (turgor from the vacuole) and self-feeding (chloroplasts).
medium.analogy: Plants solved the standing-still life with three add-ons: a frame, a reservoir and a solar array.
medium.examPointer: Say 'permanent' vacuole — dropping the word blurs the animal/plant contrast the table draws.

check.stem: Which THREE structures do plant cells have that animal cells lack?
Why do leaf cells keep the cell turgid via the vacuole?

options.text: The sap presses the cytoplasm outward onto the wall
options.explanation: The note states this pressing mechanism.

options.text: In every plant cell including roots

options.explanation: The note scopes chloroplasts to leaf and stem tissue.

check.stem: A diagram shows a cell with a nucleus, mitochondria, a cellulose wall and a permanent vacuole but NO chloroplasts. Best call?

options.text: A plant cell from tissue without photosynthetic role, such as a root
options.explanation: Wall + vacuole make it plant; missing chloroplasts scopes it away from leaves.

options.text: An animal cell, because chloroplasts are missing
options.explanation: Walls and vacuoles rule out animal.

options.text: A bacterium, because chloroplasts are missing
A fungus, because of the wall
options.explanation: Fungi lack the permanent vacuole in this course's model.

check.stem: Name the material that builds plant cell walls.
check.modelAnswer: Cellulose — the material that builds the wall.

check.stem: State the two cell structures that BOTH animal and plant cells contain for releasing energy and building protein.
Explain why the cell wall and the cell membrane are NOT interchangeable in a labelled diagram.
check.modelAnswer: The wall is the rigid cellulose outer layer giving shape and protection, while the membrane is the thin selective barrier controlling traffic; one is structural scaffolding, the other the gatekeeper, so a diagram that labels one where the other belongs misstates the cell's design.

check.stem: A pondweed sample's cells look flaccid under the microscope after salt water is added. Using the plant-cell structures, explain the observation.
check.modelAnswer: Salt water draws water out, so the permanent vacuole loses cell sap and stops pressing the cytoplasm against the cellulose wall — the cell goes flaccid, showing the vacuole's turgor role.

glossary.definition: The watery solution of dissolved substances inside the permanent vacuole.
Describes a plant cell swollen firm because the vacuole presses the cytoplasm against the wall.
The subcellular structure where proteins are synthesised.
